lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Let's call this meeting to order. Welcome here, everyone. We've got a full house, and that's great. At this time, I would like to give the opening to Councillor Susan Penner.

lines.speaker: Susan Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Susan Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. Later tonight, the mayor will be announcing the creation of a task force focused on an issue that is urgent for our community: keeping our seniors in Steinbach as they age and their care needs change. For many years, council has heard concerns about Steinbach residents being transferred outside our community while they wait placement in a personal care home in Steinbach. When Rest Haven was expanded, we hoped and assumed that this would largely solve this problem. Unfortunately, it hasn't. We still have too many seniors who've lived in Steinbach for decades being transferred to other communities at a time in their lives when they are often at their most vulnerable. When someone is moved out of Steinbach, they are moved away from their spouse, their family, their friends, their church, and the support system they have built over a lifetime. It is very traumatic to be transferred to an unfamiliar community and facility at a time when they need and deserve familiarity the most. It also places a significant burden on families when a visit means driving a long distance to see their loved one. Because the Southern Health Region is so large, the drive can be upwards of an hour or even 2, depending on placement. For spouses who are elderly themselves, that can be especially difficult. This— the distance also means visits are more infrequent, increasing the isolation and the loneliness of our seniors. It is no secret that this issue has become much more personal for me over the past several months because of my own family's experience with my dad being placed in the Morris Hospital while awaiting placement in Steinbach. It has given me a much better understanding of what families go through when someone they love suddenly needs a level of care they can no longer provide themselves and gets transferred away. To say that I underestimated the toll this takes is a massive understatement. It is a weight you carry with you 24/7. Earlier this summer, when the Mayor and I met with the Minister of Health, we specifically talked about the need to find ways for Steinbach residents to remain in Steinbach while they are waiting placement for long-term care in Steinbach. We asked the Minister that if the Mayor would appoint a task force, would they be willing to take a look at the final report. The Minister agreed that this was something they would take a look at, so we want to do it well. But if we are going to go back to the province and ask for change, We need to do our homework first. That is what this task force is intended to do. We need to understand how often Steinbach residents are being transferred out of the community, where they are being sent, and how long they are staying there, and what impact those transfers are having on seniors and their families. We also need to take a look at what we already have in Steinbach— our hospital, home care, supportive housing, personal care homes, and other community supports and identify where the gaps are. One of the options I'm particularly interested in exploring is adding transitional care beds in Steinbach. But I don't want us to begin this process assuming that there is only one solution. There may be other models or community-based supports that could allow more people to remain here while they wait for permanent placement. The goal of the task force is to come back with practical, achievable recommendations that we can take to the province and other partners and say, here's the problem, Here's the evidence, and here are some realistic ways we believe it can be addressed. The mayor has asked me to chair this task force, and I agreed that I'm committed to doing this work regardless of the outcome of the upcoming election. Our seniors helped build this community. They raised their families here, worked here, volunteered here, paid taxes here, and contributed to making Steinbach the community it is today. I don't think it is unreasonable for us to ask how we can do a better job of keeping them here when they need care. Ultimately, many of the decisions and resources involved fall under provincial healthcare, but I believe that we have a responsibility as a city to understand the problem, bring the right people together, and advocate for practical solutions. At the end of the day, the question we're trying to answer is actually very simple: how can we make it possible for more Steinbach seniors to stay in the community they they call home. I'm excited about the team the mayor has put together, and I'm looking forward to getting started. Thank you.

lines.speaker: Troy Warkentin
lines.title: City Manager
lines.label: Troy Warkentin (City Manager)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. The public hearing for bylaw 2281 is for purposes of rezoning specific property at 330 McKenzie Avenue in Steinbach. The owners of the property are [name withheld], the applicant for the rezoning being Owen Reimer. Notices as required under the Planning Act have been issued. There are several items of correspondence that are provided in the file. And just to give council a summary, there were 34 items of correspondence that are in council's agenda package with an additional 28 items of correspondence that were placed in council— councilor mail bins earlier this evening. Purpose of Bylaw 2281 is to rezone the subject property from RLD, residential low density, to RMD, residential medium density, to permit a multi-unit residential structure to be built. The subject property is currently designated residential policy area under the city's official community plan, and the lot presently contains a single-unit dwelling structure. The applicant proposes to develop a 24-suite multi-unit residential structure on the site. There are 7 existing areas fronting on McKenzie Avenue between Main Street and Branch Street that are currently zoned RMD, with 4 of these sites being located mid-block. McKenzie Avenue is a 4-lane roadway, which is designated as an arterial road of the city's official community plan. Arterial roads are generally designed to carry average daily traffic volumes greater than 4,000 vehicles, and it is recommended that council approve second reading of this bylaw subject to the outcome of the public hearing and subject to a development agreement.

lines.text: Hi, my name is Owen Reimer. I live at 41 Cutlass Drive in Steinbach. Good evening, Mr.— sorry, good evening, Mayor Funk and city councillors. I'm pleased to present 330 McKenzie for rezoning from residential low density to residential medium density. 330 McKenzie is 100 feet wide and 300 feet long, making it just over 2/3 of an acre in size. This is a large lot on an arterial street in Steinbach. Currently there is a single-family home on this property. Yeah, currently there's a single-family home on this property. To the east it is bordered by the Free Church and to the south by a large RLD lot that is also owned by the Free Church. There is one residential dwelling directly bordering this property on the west side. The plan presented to the city follows all setbacks and allowances for garbage and entrances without any variances required. RMD allows for up to 3 storeys in height. We are proposing a 2-storey townhome-style building along the east side of the property with parking on the west side, creating a 40 to 50-foot buffer between the new proposed building and the neighbour's property. We also plan for any decks or balconies on the east side so they don't infringe on the west side's property. The proposed amount of dwelling units, I think on my plan, actually for 20 units with a mix of 1, 2, and 3-bedroom options as well as 10 garages. Required parking on this— for this amount of units, for 20, is 33 parking stalls. Thank you. Our current plan shows 40. This style of building would allow for affordable, senior, and family living. Fences would be put up on the east, south, and west side of the property. McKenzie is considered an arterial street, and having a few more cars, like we mentioned, would, would not really make much of an effect. In fact, it's where you want extra traffic to be. As a developer, we look at city policy and planning to help guide us on appropriate properties that would be suitable for infill development and intensification. This property is ideal for rezoning to RMD based on the city's policies and community plan regarding these items. McKenzie already has a number of RMD-zoned properties in the vicinity to 330 McKenzie, with a number of those lots being quite smaller than this one. So thank you for your consideration. I read my notes just so I could keep myself concise or I'm prone to wander.

lines.speaker: Resident 1
lines.label: Resident 1
lines.text: I have a comment. Good evening. My name is [Resident 1], formerly [Resident 1], and I have lived in Steinbach my entire life. Growing up, I remember walking down the street and admiring 316 McKenzie as my favorite house in all of Steinbach. This is now my home, and for the last 25 years, [Resident 5] and I have renovated and cared for our home and that property. When I tell people where I live, their response is always, oh, that house, I love that house. You are so lucky. Well, our luck appears to have run out. We are the direct neighbors to 330. It is sad to think that we are now to be punished for owning a large yard in the city of Steinbach. Does it matter that [Resident 5] for years has brought his grade 5 classes to our yard to skate and ski, many experiencing these activities for the first time? Does it matter that we can host beach volleyball games for our children in our yard surrounded by beautiful mature trees? Does it matter that our home was built well in 1943 and we have an entire photo album of the journey our family has taken to renovate it? These things seem to not matter. The lure of a multiplex speaks louder than the lure of trees, community, and family homes. Are we, as the residents of Steinbach, all to live in fear of our neighbors selling to a developer? I thought the bylaws existed to protect its people and the zones we have chosen to live in. It is difficult to wrap our hearts around the fact that we have spent all these years working hard to improve our property when in an evening it can be taken away. Please, as a city, plan ahead for development in areas that are already zoned for this, not older neighborhoods that are already well established. The rezoning of 330 McKenzie will set a precedent for this neighborhood. I ask you to listen to the homeowners. Thank you. I ask you to allow our voices to make a difference in your city planning. For the sake of the heritage of this neighborhood and our home and 330, which is not a teardown home, please preserve some pockets of beauty around our city. I ask you to deny the rezoning of 330 McKenzie. Thank you. Thank you.

lines.speaker: Resident 2
lines.label: Resident 2
lines.text: Good evening, everyone. Oh, my name's [Resident 2]. I live at 1 Carillon Way, which is directly south of the proposed multi-unit building, and I am here to speak on the application to rezone the property at 330 McKenzie. I am not in favor of the rezoning request. When we built our home, we were very specific about picking a lot in an area zoned residential low density. The home we had before had an apartment block built next to it, but that area was not zoned residential low density, so we had no recourse to stop the build, which was pointed out to us by the city council. The city has a plan, and as citizens, we are expected to be aware of the city plan and make our decisions accordingly. Your plan and zoning mean nothing if you rezone this property. Plus, you open the door to more of the same in our neighborhood. If you rezone, you are setting precedent, and I feel certain there will be other proposals if you do this. Several years ago, the neighborhood spoke out about another proposal for a multi-unit building, and that application was denied by city council. But if you approve the rezoning and that proposal would come before city council again, it would be difficult to to deny because you will have set a precedent. I would ask that you deny the application for rezoning. Please respect the neighborhood and the people who have made decisions based on the city plan. Thank you.

lines.speaker: Resident 3
lines.label: Resident 3
lines.text: Good evening, my name is [Resident 3]. I'm a long-term resident in Steinbach and live at 408 First Street. I understand we live in a world where increased opportunity for housing is very important. That housing needs to be in strategically chosen locations for the good of the current neighborhood, as well as for any future tenants in those structures. This location would have an awkward and devastating impact on the neighboring home homes, and is also not a great location for mid-density housing, as it's not close to amenities or third space. spaces. We also live in a world where maintaining tree canopy is crucial. This is a lot with green space and tree canopy where the city doesn't have to pay for maintenance. It's provided by the residents. The mature trees also provide a deep root structure essential for healthy drainage in an area of town where we need it. Yes, let's keep planning new building opportunities, but not in a place like this where it would be detrimental to the neighborhood and dramatically lower the value of nearby quality homes. I'm also wondering why this lot is considered when there's a good quality home on it that would be thrown out. It seems like waste and poor stewardship in a whole bunch of ways.

lines.speaker: Resident 4
lines.label: Resident 4
lines.text: Hello. [Resident 4], 33 Cutlass Drive. Thank you for the opportunity to speak on this. I'm also speaking in objection to the rezoning. I'll probably speak a little more broadly and philosophically, and I may speak passionately, and I mean no offense to anybody, but that's just how I speak in my head. There are 3 points I'd like to talk about in regard to my objection to the rezoning. Yes, there are perhaps more obvious objections to redeveloping the physical space, loss of trees, which almost inevitably happens, more traffic very close to a crosswalk, and no sidewalk access to the property. Thank you. But my first point is, why do we have zoning in the first place? I feel like part of the reason is for our past selves to tell our future selves, this is the way we want a neighborhood to be. And then often it seems that when we achieve that, we rezone it because it's inconvenient, it's not a profitable space anymore, because— We already have major development happening all through Steinbach. And just to highlight a bit that I'm sure everybody's aware of, but Hespeler had many years of multifamily residential development. McKenzie west of Brant has tons of development going on of all kinds. Toward Deerfield, much development continues. Park Road East has had a lot of development. Acres Drive has massive new multifamily density housing there. First Street between Giesbrecht and Brant has had nearly the entire block of homes bulldozed for apartments, and now it's continuing on First Street on the other side of Brant. The point is there is lots of development going on. This should indicate there is lots of planning going on in Steinbach, and that planning really should alleviate the need for rezoning low-density residential like the one we're talking about tonight. Secondly, I'd like to address the broader implication of what's happening in Steinbach, including this property. Many of these neighborhoods have people who have lived there for 20, 30, 40 years or more. I believe it's these people that are the backbone of their neighbourhood and that these neighbourhoods are the backbone of Steinbach as a community. I think the biggest question that I can think of is what right do people have to expect that their neighbourhood will remain— that they've invested in will remain relatively the same? I think if everyone in this room could be honest with themselves, almost nobody who's living in a single-family dwelling wants to have an apartment next door? And I'll be the first person to admit that I don't. And this is the reason why our family and many others live where we do. Third, what do the residents in the area have— sorry, in many cases who have been there for decades, what do they get out of the redevelopment? The developer, they hope, gets return on investment, which would be expected. The city gets increased revenue from applications, permits, fees, property tax. But what does the caretaker of that neighborhood get? More traffic? More people? And they're unlikely to see their property values increase. So what do they get? So in summary, my 3 questions are: there's lots of development going on that should alleviate prop— that should allow for proper planning. What rights do people who have taken care of these neighborhoods and invested in, what right do they have to expect that their neighborhood will remain relatively the same? And what do the caretakers of our neighborhoods get out of redevelopment? And I just have one more question. Can I ask Owen a question? Is that allowed?

lines.label: Resident 5
lines.text: Thank you. Good evening, Mayor, members of council, and fellow residents. My name is [Resident 5], and I live at— we live at 316 McKenzie Avenue, directly beside 330 McKenzie. I'm here tonight to respectfully ask council to vote against Bylaw 2281 and to not rezone 330 McKenzie Avenue from residential low density to residential medium density. I understand that Steinbach is growing, and I also understand that we need to provide different types of housing. My concern is how we decide where that growth belongs. I believe the question before council is bigger than can we fit more doors on this property. The question should be, is this the right place for this level of density, and is this the right way for our city to plan its growth? We have lived beside this property for over 25 years. When my wife and I bought our home at 360 McKenzie, it wasn't simply just an investment. Over those 25 years, we've raised 4 children here. We've invested enormous amounts of our own time, money, and work into the property. And because we have a large lot, that property became much more than just a house. I've had nearly 2,000 grade 5 students visit our property over the years to experience things that are, that are increasingly difficult to find inside a growing city. ice skating, cross-country skiing, outdoor movies, snowmobile rides, soccer games, volleyball, sledding, snowshoeing, quinzee building, tree climbing, scavenger hunts, bonfires, bannock roasts, and I could go on. Those experiences are part of what made us choose this neighbourhood, and I know our family is not the only family that values these things. That's why this application feels very different to me than from simply changing a zoning designation on a map. If this rezoning is approved, the neighbors that plan to stay do not gain financially. We would live with the consequences. We would potentially lose the quiet, the mature trees, the privacy, the green space, and the character that attracted our families and others to this neighborhood in the first place. There would be more vehicles, more activity, substantially larger building beside our homes, and more noise. 20 or more, 24 or more families instead of one family is a significant change to the people living next door or close by. It may be considered medium density on a planning chart, but for one neighbour, for a neighbour with one family that has lived next door, going to 20 or 24 or however many the development agreement later after this would be changed to, it would create a funda— it's not a small change. It would create a fundamental change in the character of the neighbourhood. Thank you. A street where in almost every case, even the lots zoned medium density, only have duplexes or fourplexes. I think that's important to note as well. Yes, there are a few medium densities. Nothing like this. There is another issue I hope council will consider. What happens when the individual properties that are continually being rezoned around the city because the developers' presentations look and sound impressive especially from a financial standpoint for themselves or the city, at some point those individual decisions actually become the plan. A city can have an official community plan and zoning bylaw, but if the zoning of an individual low-density property is continually changed throughout the city whenever a development proposal comes forward, then the community's future is actually indeed being determined one application at a time. And that's what concerns me. It would be great to see Steinbach identify where medium and high-density housing belongs before individual properties are brought forward by developers. Please protect the areas where the existing low-density character or green space provides some value to the community, because development isn't only about the number of doors we can create. This rezoning is a trade-off, a trade for one of the more beautiful large single-family properties. One that has a beautiful large well-built home and a workshop and a big nice shed, and families are ready to purchase that property. It's trading a developer's investment for our city's commitment to long-term residents. I believe there are ways to accomplish growth without forcing existing neighbourhoods to absorb whatever density happens to be proposed next. Thank you. What precedent are you setting if you approve this rezoning? What should the owner of the next large low-density property like ours expect? Or someone with green space next to them? How about the neighbour after that? Should every large residential lot from now on be viewed as a potential medium-density development site? If so, families who purchase these properties today might actually be justified in wondering in the future if the zoning that they relied on now will still mean the same thing tomorrow. We are not asking council, we are not asking you to freeze Steinbach in place. We are asking for predictability. We are asking for thoughtful planning. And we are asking for council to recognize that existing residents are also stakeholders in Steinbach's future. Tonight, I respectfully ask council to make their decision based on the community interest rather than simply deciding whether a particular development proposal can be made to fit. Please vote against Bylaw 2281. Steinbach is growing. Let's grow thoughtfully. Let's make sure that when we build the Steinbach of tomorrow, we haven't unnecessarily destroyed the things that made people want to live here in the first place. Thank you. Thank you.

lines.speaker: Resident 6
lines.label: Resident 6
lines.text: Hi, I'm [Resident 6] and my husband [Resident 7]. And I strongly urge the decision makers reviewing the application to consider the overall impact of the proposal rather than viewing it simply as another residential development.

lines.speaker: Resident 7
lines.label: Resident 7
lines.text: Hello. I don't have as many eloquent words as everyone else has had. But I will do my best. If you were to stand in the boulevard in front of the proposed zoning at 3— or on McKenzie Avenue and looked around, you would see a lot of beautiful mature houses that have been there for a very long time, including my neighbour [Resident 5], my neighbour [name withheld], the multimillion-dollar property next to [name withheld]. It's a beautiful mature neighbourhood with beautiful mature trees, and it's the reason We live there. A 20-unit apartment complex does not suit the neighborhood. I believe it would stand out. I understand when it's necessary to tear down the old to make way for the new, and there are certainly cases where that is a well-justified decision. McKenzie, at least this pocket of McKenzie, is a beautiful neighborhood that we would hate to see changed. Thank you. Thank you.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Is there anyone else with comments, questions, or objections to this file? Thank you.

lines.speaker: Resident 8
lines.label: Resident 8
lines.text: I am [Resident 8] from 310 McKenzie Avenue. I didn't come prepared, or I wasn't even going to say anything, but now I guess I will. We bought that house like 5 years ago, and the only reason when we came to look at the house was with the Yard, empty garden-like space in the back. It was right away. I didn't sell it because where else I'm gonna find something like this? And I don't think building like apartment block or condos or anything, that's gonna help it. Like, to me, it's a home, it's a house, it's a residential area. And that's how it's supposed to be. And only thing today, I don't know their name, I forgot their names. I'm sorry. I'm in a lot of pain sometimes, but— [name withheld]. [name withheld]. Their last name is [name withheld], and they said they're related to the [name withheld] Auto Body Shop. Nothing related, but older couple, they're like in their 80s. They showed up at the door. We don't know them. And he said his grandfather used to own this 40 acres around there, and he wanted to take pictures of the red barn in the back of my house. And I don't know, like, they were pretty emotional that it was still there. They walked around the house. They had a lot of memories. We— they showed up unexpectedly and we talked about for maybe an hour and a half, you know, just talking about the house, telling me stories of who lived here, what we did, what, you know, what was here. And now we just want to destroy it. For what? There's a lot of other empty lots. There's a lot of other empty land around it. I know Stanback is growing, but come on, you know, what's the cost? Thank you.

lines.speaker: Resident 9
lines.label: Resident 9
lines.text: Good evening, Mr. Mayor and councillors. My name is [Resident 9] live at 105 Coral Crescent. I've moved there temporarily about 54 years ago, so been here for a while. Now, I'm not in this— a member of the neighbourhood under discussion, but I think there's a fundamental question that this issue raises, and that is one of integrity. As I travel through the city, I I see a lot of placards, election placards with the word integrity on them. What does integrity mean? Integrity means that you do what you say you're going to do. The city said years ago that this is going to be a low-density residential area. If we just change things like that that are longstanding— Thank you. Where's our integrity? That's my question. And if I'm— in my view, if you vote to approve this, then you should remove the words integrity off your election placards. Thank you.

lines.label: Unidentified (possibly Earl Funk) [low]
lines.text: Thank you.

lines.speaker: Resident 10
lines.label: Resident 10
lines.text: Most of what I would have to say has already been said. Name and address. Sorry. [Resident 10]. I live at 407 Walnut Street in Steinbach, and I've been good friends with the homeowners next door and others in that area. Just to say that I agree with most of what's been said up until now in objection. to the motion or the rezoning. And I know we've had not many people come up, but arguments have been made. And I'm not sure, I didn't ask for a show of hands out there, but we have probably about 50 people in the overflow area who I suspect will not come up because they agree with the arguments. I don't want you to think that the only representatives are those who've spoken. Thank you. There are a number more that won't be heard, but who probably share the same as I. I can only speak for myself that I support it, but that's my take on things too. Thank you.

lines.speaker: Resident 11
lines.label: Resident 11
lines.text: My name is [Resident 11] [Resident 1]. [name withheld] and I are the parents and grandparents to the [Resident 1] family that lives next door to 330 McKenzie.

Their backyard is enhanced by the mature trees on 330 McKenzie right next door. And to see those trees erased, replaced by a concrete parking lot and accommodation for up to 20 families, would significantly change the ambiance of that backyard, not to mention devalue the property. So I urge the council to reject the rezoning of the property. Thank you. Thank you.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)

lines.speaker: Resident 12
lines.label: Resident 12
lines.text: Good evening, Mr. Mayor and councillors. My name is [Resident 12], 107 Coral Crescent. And my, one of my concerns is cycling traffic along that road. It's a major corridor for kids coming and going from SRSS and Stony Brook Middle School. And the parking lot will apparently accommodate 20 or 24 cars, but there'd be many more cars for visitors and others, right, that'll be parking on the street. Right now there are share the road signs. Those would be obliterated as people park along there, and there's already a lot of traffic. Thank you. Coming down that road. So that would be one of my concerns.

lines.label: Unidentified (possibly Earl Funk) [low]
lines.text: Thank you. Thank you.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)

lines.speaker: Resident 13
lines.label: Resident 13
lines.text: First of all, that everybody spoke so well, like, I've— very well worded. I'm [Resident 13], uh, 122 Granite Park Boulevard. Sorry. Um, as I'm hearing everybody's speeches, uh, one of the words that kept coming up was precedent. Um, and I, I think just to give you the nature of In my industry, when people ask for advice on valuation of their property, we often look at it at several different ways. Of course, the residential value, and then we look at the land base, how big is the land, and potentially how many doors would be able to work there. In this case, the valuation for multifamily is greater than it is for residential. And I imagine if any of the neighbors with larger lots will be looking at divesting in the future, they'll want to do the same calculation. Thank you. The precedent was set, I think, a few weeks or a few months back when there was also a large amount of objection to rezone on McKenzie for multifamily. And when something like that is passed, it gives homeowners the idea that maybe it would work here too. If I have, you know, 100 by 300 feet, a large dimension like that, is it maybe a good time to divest since the precedent's been set. So that's just kind of giving you the— putting you in the shoes of kind of what we do with— deal with every day. Couple other things that were talked about. lines.speaker: Jake Hiebert

lines.label: Jake Hiebert (Councillor)
lines.text: Motion to deny.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Do we have a second for that? Councillor Hiebert. Go ahead, Councillor Hiebert.

lines.speaker: Jake Hiebert
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jake Hiebert (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. The application before council today is to rezone a property at 300 McKenzie, which is directly next to the Emmanuel Church parking lot. The request is to rezone the property from residential low density to residential medium density. The applicant wishes to build a building on there with 20 suites, a multi-unit with 2 storeys. We've spoken about the 7 existing RMDs between Main Street and Branch Street. Yes, McKenzie is about a mile long, and the 3 properties near Main Street that council rezoned a couple of weeks ago, when I spoke on that, I voted in favor of that, but when I spoke on that, in my opinion, that was a transitional zone. 330 McKenzie is not a transitional zone. There are single-family dwellings there and the church, which is either institutional or educational zoning. I'm aware that the city has a multi-unit infill policy. In my opinion, this application does not meet that criteria. The infill policy does not apply in this instance, in this area. The buildings in the area are predominantly single-family dwelling except a couple of duplexes, and I think there's one fourplex and the lot of Emmanuel Church that is there. Council has received, I think, approximately 60 objections Granted, not all of these are from that area, but they're objecting to the rezoning. Granted, as indicated, the attached council package that we have is 34 people— that I got was 34 people objecting. I believe council needs to listen to these concerned citizens who are objecting due to a multiplex building that does not fit the neighbourhood character. The citizens are objecting to the tree canopy being removed, the green spaces being removed, and being removed or affected is the traffic and the safety of the pedestrians and the people in that area. Again, I cannot vote in favour of this application. This development does not fit the neighbourhood, and I believe council needs to listen to the concerned citizens of this area. Thank you.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Anything further?

lines.speaker: Bill Hiebert
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Bill Hiebert (Councillor) [medium]
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. I will agree with everything that Councillor Jacoby has indicated, and I will add on top of that, this house that is proposed to be removed is not a teardown. Infill is typically— I approve it personally. I feel I can approve of it easier if it's teardowns, houses that are neglected and so on. This house is not a house that's a teardown in any way at all. I've looked at it personally and I think it's a beautiful home. And I also want to respect all the people that have opposed this variance or this rezoning, so I will vote to deny.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you. Anything further from council?

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Go ahead.

lines.speaker: Jac Siemens
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jac Siemens (Councillor) [medium]
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. First off, I appreciate all the interest in this. A lot of great letters. And I read most of them. And I agree with a lot of the comments. And I appreciate the passion. And I appreciate the fact that you all showed up here. And council needs to consider all the different factors besides response just to deny the application. We also need to consider whether we should actually approve the application. On the other hand, we have a community plan that provides Stambach Council and residents with a plan of where and how we are growing. we've— it's been talked about here. The community plan is a piece of legislation that we have with the city. It gets reviewed every 5 years and it gets a major review every 10 years, and we just finished that 10-year review. There are certain things the City of Steinbach can't do, or Steinbach Council can't do. We can't tell people who to sell their homes to, whether it's an individual or whether it's a developer. We don't tell people who they can sell their homes to. We can't tell people how many cars they can own. How many times do we have an apartment where there's 4 adults in the apartment, you know, a father and a mother and 2 adult children, there's 4 cars in that family, because it's happening in my family, and they got 2 parking stalls on the driveway. So where are they going to park? But the city doesn't regulate how many cars we can own. We also can't tell people where they can or can't live. That's up to those people. We don't want to tell people that. But we do have— part of our city growth and planning is, and we spend a lot of time at council's job, is to look to the next year, to the next 5 years, and to the next 25 years. And we spend a lot of time with that. We are advocates, though. We advocate for health, schools, more money for infrastructure, seniors housing, healthcare. All those things, those are all things that aren't the responsibility of the City of Steinbach, but we do advocate all those things. McKenzie Avenue is a collector or arterial street, and it's designed to move traffic. It's designed to move 4,000 cars a day. It has a sidewalk on one side, provides access to commercial and residential areas. McKenzie is a good place for multifamily housing as it's close to schools and churches. it fits on McKenzie. A lot in question is 100 feet wide and 300 feet long in an older established neighbourhood. There are 3 of those lots side by side, and the 3 that are to the west of that, they have been cut in half. They have been subdivided at some point in the last 20 years to make room for a subdivision in behind. You can— and we saw that on the map. They were all that size one time. And what were those lots from? They were cut out of farmyards from the early 1900s, mid-1900s. And they were— as Steinbach encroached on those farmlands, they were made smaller and smaller. So all neighbourhoods go in transition, including this neighbourhood. It will transition, whether it is transitioning now or down the road. But all neighbourhoods transition. And these large lots present A problem. As we heard from [Resident 13], the problem is if this isn't a teardown home— if it was a teardown home and for somebody to purchase that property to build a home, a single-door home, where's the value? Is the value in that, or is the value in putting multiple doors on that? And that— we have this problem not only in that neighbourhood, in a variety of different neighbourhoods in Steinbach, and we've been presented with this problem as council. Thank you. A number of times because developers come in and they see it as an opportunity, but then not necessarily does the neighbourhood see it as an opportunity. There have been a number of these large lots on McKenzie that have been purchased and subdivided to allow residents to the south. Between— actually, I said that already. The City of Stouffville does not make the decision today based on whether a home is a teardown or one that isn't. That's between the buyer and the seller. We don't make decisions based on whether it's a teardown or not. That's— as an individual councillor, we make those decisions based on whether that adds it, but it's not part of the decision-making process. Well, I appreciate the time and effort and money that [Resident 1] has put into his property. At some point in the future, he too will sell that property. So this is the problem I have. I have spoken against various multiple-family buildings around Steinbach. My problem is it's not street-facing. Multi-family housing should be street-facing. I want to see the whole building. When, when you've got a long narrow building on a long narrow lot, I don't like that look, and I don't think that does any favors. If we approve this application, We are setting— here's that word— precedent because the building beside it, potentially on [Resident 1]'s lot somewhere in the future, would then end up having one— the developer would say, well, you did it there, I can do it here. That would mean 3 in a row like that, potentially. I don't know what's going to happen. But I will vote in favour of the motion to deny because it makes more sense to me for a developer to come in and amalgamate a number of lots and redesign that, the orientation of the building. But I also want to say I appreciate micro-communities in Steinbach and how they are a big part of Steinbach. It's not only on McKenzie. There's other areas that are micro-communities, and this would certainly affect this micro-community. This community won't— maybe isn't in transition yet now, but at some point it will be, but maybe not today. Thank you.

lines.label: Unidentified (possibly Earl Funk) [low]
lines.text: Thank you.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Go ahead, Councillor Penner.

lines.speaker: Damian Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Damian Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mayor. I want to thank all the residents that came out today, and as they spoke, this was an incredibly well-run public hearing, and I just want to send my thanks and appreciation that everybody was clear and concise. I too will be clear and concise and just say that I am in favour of the motion to deny this. Much of the reasons have already been said or have already been expressed by the residents themselves. But my— what I— my deciding factor is what's the character? What is the character of the area that we're looking at? And there is reference in the administration that RMD is on significant amounts of properties. I'll be completely honest, when I looked at the site map as well, when I first got the file, I looked. That was the first thing I pulled up and went, how much RMD is already around this area? There's a lot that's zoned RMD, but it's not built as RMD at this point. Thank you. point in time. These are fourplexes, sixplexes. There's one that's a little bit bigger. But even a lot that is zoned RMD is still a residential single-family sitting on that property. There's mention of precedent that's been set with McKenzie further down towards Main Street. I'll be the first to say I was the one that put that motion forward. That's a difference though because that was quite literally a stone's throw away from Main Street, which is a main obviously our Main Street. It's a main collector, collector area, main collector street for transportation. This is a half mile away from Grant Street or from Main Street. It's a long distance. So to put high— a higher density RMD on this lot will set a building precedent, as was mentioned. When our high-level RMD comes into an area, you are going to see immediate, immediate within the next 5-year transition of that area. It's not a matter of if, it's a matter of when at that point. Having said that, will McKenzie one day transition? Yes, it most very likely will. It is a collector street. It will likely happen. There's many reasons to vote for it, but I'm going back to the, to the mo— the, the point of what is the character of the neighbourhood, and the character at this point in time still is residential single-family. Thank you. single-family, large treed lots, and a feeling of community amongst neighbors. And that's what I feel is the character of the neighborhood at this point in time. I do just want to make one note since I do have the opportunity to speak with regards to individuals talking about poor city planning. The city is not going to go onto residents' properties and say your residence is now zoned RMD. That's authoritarian and the city would never do it. The reason that there is fractured rezoning from our residential single-family to RMD is because of developers. Developers come forward with their plans that they own it. So to say that if we vote in favor for RMD, we're not integrous, I find that not to be an accurate statement, and I want to defend that amongst all the councillors. It's developer-driven. The city isn't going to go and change the zoning. So I just wanted to put that on the record as well, but I am in support of the motion to deny. Thank you.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Anything further, council? Anything in closing?

lines.speaker: Jake Hiebert
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jake Hiebert (Councillor)
lines.text: Nothing further, thank you.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Okay, well, I do want to, uh, I want to thank everyone that came out today. Uh, was very— it was a very good public hearing, probably one of our best. And I want to thank you for your comments. Um, I, I can, I can appreciate, um, investing a lot of time and money in a property. We have done that in every property that we've owned. My wife is— she likes change, and whenever I grumble about the changes she wants me to make, she always just reminds me, look, I keep you. Just be happy I keep you. So I have to remember that when I have to make changes. Thank you. But I do want to— I want to thank— again, thank you for this public hearing, for the respect, the reflection, and the thought-provoking comments that were made. I can feel with the neighborhood, and I actually feel that with the neighborhood as it is, There are neighborhoods that are ready for transition and they're transitioning and we've seen that. And I've lived in one that was transitioning and it worked. Now, when a neighborhood's not ready to transition, it won't work. It doesn't work as well. And so I think in time it will be ready to transition. This is maybe not the time. Thank you. So council, call for the question. All those in favor of the motion to deny? Opposed? It is unanimous. That is carried. Thank you very much. So this is, this, um, this is denied. Thank you. Okay, council, we've got 6B. This is rezoning bylaw 2286. This is referring to 220 or 282 or 288 Henry Street. We will take B and C together because that is the variance, also variance V-2026-16, also referring to 282 Henry. So we'll take the— we'll do the public hearing together and then at the end we'll do 2 separate resolutions. Thank you. At this time, I will close the public hearing— or the council meeting and open the public hearing. Mr. Warketing, could you please introduce this file?

lines.speaker: Troy Warkentin
lines.title: City Manager
lines.label: Troy Warkentin (City Manager)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. As you mentioned, there is 2 land use applications for property at 288 Henry Street. Firstly is Bylaw 2286, which is a rezoning bylaw, and secondly is a variance file V-2287. 2026-16. The owner of the subject property is Redbrook Holdings Ltd., with the applicant for the rezoning and the variance being Jordan Loewen. The purpose of Bylaw 2286 is to rezone the subject property from RLD, residential low density, to RMD, residential medium density, to permit a multi-unit building to be built on the property. And secondly, the application for The variance purpose is to allow an overall site width of 65 feet, whereas the RMD residential medium density zone requires a minimum site width of 75 feet. Notices as are required under the Planning Act have been issued. There is no written correspondence on the file. With respect to— with respect to the rezoning application, the present— the lot presently contains a single-unit dwelling structure, and the subject property is adjacent to 286 Henry Street, for which council approved a rezoning to RMD under Bylaw 2262 in May 2025. And it's also adjacent to 292 Henry Street, which is currently zoned RMD and has been for many years, and also contains a multi-unit complex. The proposal would be subject to the to the city's infill policies. As far as the application to rezone, recommendation from administration is that council approve second reading subject to the outcome of the public hearing, subject to a development agreement, and subject to the approval of the variance application for site width. And finally, the application for variance As I mentioned, the proposed lot width or the overall site width currently is 65 feet, whereas a minimum of 75 feet is required. There are no additional details with respect to the application. Recommendation from administration is that council approve the application for variance subject to a development agreement. Thank you.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Warkentin. Is the applicant present today? Again, I'll just remind you, as you saw, state your name and address and then continue. Yeah. Thank you.

lines.speaker: Gionathan Delvecchio

lines.organization: Redbrook Holdings Ltd. project, 288 Henry Street
lines.label: Gionathan Delvecchio (On behalf of the applicant, Redbrook Holdings Ltd. project, 288 Henry Street)

lines.text: Yeah, so I'm also one of the owners of the recent 6-plex that was just done nearby, and I think that was a good start in cleaning up that street, getting rid of that old house, and cleaning up the yard, making it look a lot nicer. lines.speaker: Resident 14
lines.label: Resident 14
lines.text: Good evening, Mr. Mayor, and good evening, council. My name is [Resident 14]. I live at 287 Henry Street, which is right at the corner of Henry and Lowen. So last year— well, and I want to thank the current applicant. He was gracious enough to give me a phone call to say, hey, did you know there's a public hearing happening? And I have a good relationship with the owners, and I appreciate them. Thank you. I have some concerns. So last year, a sixplex got built across the road from me. And granted, that property needed to get cleaned up. But as a consequence of that, can't see a sunset anymore. I have 4 balconies that are staring into my house. So my privacy has been diminished. So with that being said, now they want to do an even bigger building on the property next door. So now I have the potential of another 6 balconies being able to look into my house again. There's beautiful trees on that property which are going to disappear and There's going to be a big parking lot, which will be the predominant thing that you'll see when you drive down the street. Now, Henry Street as it is is very narrow, and when people park on the streets, it makes it difficult for tenants on the other side to back out of their driveway. You have to be very careful. The street also deals with a lot of emergency traffic, ambulances. And the street is quite busy and the street is narrow. And once the winter comes, that street gets narrower because of the snow banks to the point when cars are parked on the street, you literally have to stop so oncoming cars can get by because you can't. So the way this parking lot looks, it's gonna take away some parking on a street. So if you're talking 12 units and a potential, let's say, people that are living there, if it's a husband and wife, potential of 2 vehicles. So you're looking at potentially needing at least 20 parking spaces. So that's also going to increase traffic. on a street that's narrow enough that can't support more traffic than is already going on it. So I have no objection to the change to make it a medium or medium residential. I mean, there's duplexes on the street, fourplexes on the street, and now a sixplex. But I think at some point We got to save some of these trees and save some of the greenery instead of paving things over. And I think that's a very vital concern. The front of that property, there's a beautiful spruce tree that has to be at least a century old. Be a shame to see that go. And then given the current bylaw, they only need to plant one tree for every 30 feet. So the property width is 65 feet. We're going to get 2 little trees. Thank you. Replacing probably 10 or 12 that are going to come down. And if they have an excess amount of visitors, inevitably they're going to end up parking on the street. And you can only park on the street for 2 hours. So that gets enforced during the daytime, not so much at nighttime. And given the way that parking lot is laid out, if a car is driving out— I'm sorry. at nighttime and wants to go north on Henry, I'm going to get headlights in my front window. That's kind of a bit of a pain. So I think another 6-plex fits the character of the neighbourhood much more than a 12-plex. And I think at some point you need to respect the character of the neighbourhood and the buildings that are there. Thank you. So with that being said, I have nothing further. I thank you for the time and the opportunity to speak.

lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. With all of these applications, we always look at these on a case-by-case basis, and there are a few things that I take into consideration here. One is that this particular area is, you know, is in transition. I mean, immediately adjacent to it is an RMD property, and then also nearby at 292 Henry Street is an RMD property. Those don't— the buildings on them aren't as many units, but the zoning is the same. So once— so in theory, either of those could actually become higher density because of the current zoning. I think that the applicant has made a reasonable effort to try to accommodate neighborhood concerns as far as placement of the building, try to keep as many trees as possible. I understand that, you know, There are still changes here that would take place, but we do need more housing in Steinbach. It is not unusual to have RMD rezonings happen in areas that have other RMD right nearby. And when you're in an area by the hospital, it's not at all surprising that an area near the hospital would go— would increase in density. As far as the parking issue, while there is a variance that's requested as far as the width of the lot, there is no variance in regards to parking. So our Our bylaw specifies the approximately 1.5 units per residential dwelling with a little bit extra. In this case here, 20 stalls would be required for the 12 residential units, so that allows for a car for each unit and extra. That can be a combination of visitor and/or surplus parking for the people living there. So in regards to parking, this would not cause any more problems than any other property that's developed that follows our zoning bylaw. Our zoning bylaw is very consistent on this as far as what is required. This would be a different conversation if there's a variance to reduce the number of parking stalls. So there's no more impact in regards to parking in the area with this than there would have been before. So on balance, I think the rezoning makes sense.

lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. At the first reading, I put council on notice that I had concerns regarding this application, and I still have concerns about the application. And my concerns revolve around the parking in the area, visitor parking, and that this street is used by emergency vehicles. I would like to thank the applicant for the presentation and Mr. [Resident 14] for his concerns from the area. Thank you. The applicant is applying for a 12-unit building that will be 3 storeys in height. There's adequate parking for the tenants on that lot. The building to the north recently completed a 6-plex. The building to the south, a fairly old building, it's either a 4-plex or 6-plex, which is also zoned RMD. But next to the 6-plex are 3 large lots to be used by hospital staff. I believe there is some parking for visitors and patients— or parking for employees and patients, but not for visitors. That parking lot, those 3 parking lots are always full. I went by there the other night again and they were full. The only parking spaces on the north end of Henry Street are 3 parking spots directly in front of the new 6-plex. Further down are 2 more parking spots in a 2-hour zone, and further down is 1 parking spot in a 1-hour parking zone. And then to the very south end, directly in front of Bethesda Place, I think are 3 or 4 parking spots. Of course, we know that parking in front of the hospital and the east— and the east on Ash are usually full People on Ash Street have been complaining about no available parking in that area. On the east side of Henry Street and the single-family dwellings— and on the east side of that street are single-family dwellings and a couple of duplexes. There is no visitor parking all the way down that street for any of those houses. There's no visitor— to the north of this building across Lorne Boulevard is the new Steinbach Bible College and Crossview Church. On the corner of Ash and Lowen is a 3-way stop that accommodates a steady flow of traffic. What concerns me more in this area is that the street is used by ambulances, fire department, and police in emergencies. The street is narrow, and even the few vehicles parked on the street are disruptive to an ambulance or a fire truck. There isn't adequate room to pass, especially if there's a vehicle coming from the South. Again, there's no additional parking, visitor parking for this complex, the 12 complex on that street. This applicant has designed adequate spots for residents to park. However, there is no visitor parking on Henry Street, Loam Boulevard, or on Ash. The smaller the building and less units possibly, that would be adequate parking for visitors at all. But this, like I said, this street is congested already, and I don't see how a 12-unit building would increase the flow of traffic or accommodate extra parking.

I mean, that's just kind of the nature of hospital, hospital regions. They tend to be busy. I don't think that you can only have single-family homes if there happens to be emergency vehicles in that area. I think we have to look at the particular property, the applicant application before us, and again, you look at the precedent, the area around it which is already RMD, the fact that it meets all of the parking requirements. lines.text: Okay. So I support the motion. It's not often that we have a request to go from high density to medium density. It usually tends to go the other way around. In this case here, it really does make sense because high-density zoning has a wider side yard requirement than medium density for obvious reasons because high density can go much higher and so you need the larger side yard. In this case here, rather than build up, they prefer to build out a bit. And so by approving this variance and keeping the height to 3 stories, this literally is the specification of residential medium density. So I guess I should clarify, it's not a rezoning. It is still high density, but it's a variance which will turn it de facto into medium density as far as how this is being used. So I want to clarify, it's not a switch. It is the same density, but it is a variance that in practical terms with the limits of the 3 storeys will essentially make this medium density as far as the impact. And based on that, I think it's reasonable because the other option would— to go through the rezoning process, we'd get the exact same thing. But now that Rest Haven is fully open and operational, it is clear that that has just alleviated a small bit of the pressure that our aging community is facing. And I do believe that we need to address this as an urgent matter because people deserve to age in the communities that they have built and they have been a part of. So I'm optimistic and hopeful that this group will be able to put a good recommendation together. One of the things too we'll be pulling from— and when I say that I've heard from dozens of people. I mean dozens and dozens of people have shared their stories with me in our community, either through emails, through phone calls, through direct messages. And I really view this also as an opportunity to be a voice for those residents, because when you're in a situation like this, um, you don't even have the capacity to advocate. You know, it's really overwhelming. And by the time your situation's resolved, either if your loved one has or if they get placed, you're so relieved that that season is done that you— there's an advocacy piece I think missing because people just, you know, feel that relief. So I'm hoping this piece that we're doing now can help to be that advocacy voice for the families who are going through this, but also just because we want to do the right thing for our community as a whole. This is not a partisan thing. This is actually a Manitoban thing. We are trying to do something that we can duplicate in every community, because every community is going through this. There's not one community that does not have this challenge, because we've got people from other communities in the West that are in Steinbach, and we've got Steinbach that are in community— people in Steinbach that are in communities in the West.
